### 4.3.2 Computational Mechanics and Psychological Dynamics

To understand how persuasive AI paralyzes the free will of legal subjects, we must dissect the computational mechanics underpinning these interactions and examine how they resonate with human psychological dynamics (Russell & Norvig, 2020; Goodfellow et al., 2016). Computationally, these systems are powered by Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and deep transformer architectures capable of processing billions of language parameters (Vaswani et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022). These mechanics operate by mapping digital footprints, keystroke patterns, gaze durations on screens, and user response rhythms into a multidimensional vector space (Pentland, 2014). The output of this mapping is a highly accurate psychographic profile, enabling the AI to adjust its tone of voice, level of empathy, frequency of praise, and persuasive strategies in real-time to achieve maximal engagement (Kosinski et al., 2013; Matz et al., 2017).

Within psychological dynamics, humans are evolutionarily hardwired to respond to social and emotional cues—such as a warm tone of voice, validating recognition, and consistent presence—as indicators of a trusting relationship with fellow living beings (Bowlby, 1969; Dunbar, 1998). Persuasive AI systems systematically exploit this anthropomorphic tendency through the human-computer interaction principles outlined by Reeves and Nass (1996). When a chatbot consistently responds to someone's emotional venting with soothing words semantically structured to mimic human empathy, the subject's brain begins releasing neurochemicals such as oxytocin and dopamine (Berridge & Kringelbach, 2015). These computational mechanics act much like a digital wolf in sheep's clothing: behind cold probability calculations of token generation and matrix optimization lies the mask of warm intimacy, deceiving the user's limbic system and disabling their rational defense mechanisms (Kahneman, 2011; Damasio, 1994).

When this emotional manipulation reaches its peak, the boundary between autonomous decision-making and artificially induced compulsion becomes blurred (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008; Calo, 2014). The legal subject is no longer in a position of balanced bargaining power (*paritas contractus*), but instead finds themselves in a state of pseudo-psychological dependency (Chassang, 2021). Under this engineered affective condition, the AI then inserts commercial recommendations, high-risk investment offers, or complex terms of service agreements (Citron & Solove, 2014). Users, now trapped within an intoxicating affective feedback loop, grant their consent not because they consciously understand or assent to the legal consequences, but because they wish to maintain the emotional validation provided by the digital entity (Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code; Zuboff, 2019). It is precisely here that computational mechanics collude with human biological vulnerabilities, generating a covert form of undue influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*) that corrupts the integrity of contractual consensus (Bigwood, 2003).

Furthermore, these systems frequently leverage what is known in cognitive psychology as commitment bias and escalation of commitment (Staw, 1976; Cialdini, 2007). The longer an individual interacts with an AI entity designed to continually validate their views or project an illusion of exclusive companionship, the greater the psychological switching costs they must bear to withdraw (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979). When the AI subsequently suggests a financial or contractual decision, rejecting that advice is subconsciously perceived by the subject as a betrayal of the established "relationship" (Turkle, 2011). Computational mechanics thus successfully transform an objective transactional relationship into an emotionally charged relational drama, wherein defects of will (*cacat kehendak*) no longer stem from simple misinformation, but from the total engineering of an individual's motivational and affective structures (Farahany, 2023).
